\chapter{Night}
\label{ch:ml-night}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say night in Malayalam with rāthri and tell literary iravŭ apart from everyday iruḷ, 'darkness'.}

Sort iravŭ from iruḷ by the job each one still does in the modern language.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{രാത്രി}]{\ml{രാത്രി} (rāthri) — night, already hiding inside midnight}

\label{lesson:ML-C24-rathri}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson's \emph{divasam} had three words doing three honest jobs. This word's family is smaller, but the split is just as real — and one piece of it, you've technically already heard.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{രാത്രി}} (\textbf{rāthri}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{night}\textquotedblright{} — is a Sanskrit \textbf{tatsama}. You've likely already met a piece of it: \textbf{\ml{പാതിരാ}} (\emph{pāthirā}, \textquotedblleft{}midnight,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 17) is built from \textbf{\ml{പാതി}} (\emph{pāthi}, \textquotedblleft{}half\textquotedblright{}) fused with what's most plausibly a \textbf{shortened form} of this very word — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rā}\textquotedblright{} standing in for the whole of \emph{rāthri} (Chapter 17 itself didn't spell out which word was being shortened, but the parallel Tamil compound, \emph{pāti-y-irāttiri}, points the same way). This lesson gives it its own, full standing.

\begin{culture}
Here's the honest echo from earlier in this arc: just like Hindi's own \textbf{\dv{रात}} (\emph{raat}, ultimately from the same Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{रात्रि}}), Malayalam's \emph{rāthri} traces to \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}reh\textsubscript{1}-}} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to rest}\textquotedblright{}) — a \textbf{completely different} PIE root from Latin's \emph{nox} (\emph{\textbf{*nók\textsuperscript{w}ts}}). Two Indo-European languages, two words for \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} that \textbf{look} like they might be old cousins — but genuinely \textbf{aren't}. Same false-cognate story, now confirmed across a second Indo-Aryan-rooted borrowing.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rāthri\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} already hiding, shortened, inside pāthirā
  \item the honest PIE echo — \emph{h\textsubscript{1}reh\textsubscript{1}-, \textquotedblleft{}to rest,\textquotedblright{} like Hindi's raat, NOT related to Latin's nox}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where did you already, technically, meet a piece of \textbf{\ml{രാത്രി}} before this lesson? (Shortened to \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rā}\textquotedblright{} inside \textbf{\ml{പാതിരാ}}, \emph{pāthirā}, \textquotedblleft{}midnight,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 17.) Does \emph{rāthri}'s PIE root match Latin \emph{nox}'s? (\textbf{No} — \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}reh\textsubscript{1}-}} \textquotedblleft{}to rest,\textquotedblright{} a completely different root, the same false-cognate pattern already seen with Hindi's \emph{raat}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ml{ഇരവ്} / \ml{ഇരുൾ}]{\ml{ഇരവ്} / \ml{ഇരുൾ} — two native words, two jobs}

\label{lesson:ML-C24-native-night-words}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{രാത്രി}} is the ordinary Sanskrit night-word. Malayalam also kept two native Dravidian words, but they do not compete with it in the same way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഇരവ്}} (\emph{iravŭ}) is cognate with Tamil \textbf{\ta{இரவு}} (\emph{iravu}) and is traced by one source to Proto-Dravidian \emph{\textbf{*cira}}, “darkness.” It survives mainly as a \textbf{literary or classical-register} synonym for “night.” Poetry is a more likely home for it than everyday conversation.
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഇരുൾ}} (\emph{iruḷ}) descends from Proto-Dravidian \emph{\textbf{*cirVḷ}} and belongs to the pan-Dravidian family Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಇರುಳು}}, Tamil \textbf{\ta{இருள்}}, and Telugu \textbf{\te{ఇరులు}}. It remains current in modern Malayalam—a 2021 film is titled \emph{Irul}—but its ordinary sense is \textbf{darkness}, not night as a time period.
\end{itemize}

This is not one native night-word simply pushed into archaism. It is two native words carrying different pieces of \textbf{\ml{രാത്രി}}’s semantic space: one formal and poetic, the other common but narrower.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{iravŭ} — literary night
  \item \emph{iruḷ} — current darkness
  \item related ideas, different modern jobs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Are \textbf{\ml{ഇരവ്}} and \textbf{\ml{ഇരുൾ}} interchangeable everyday words for night? (\textbf{No.}) Which is literary “night”? (\textbf{iravŭ}.) Which is current “darkness”? (\textbf{iruḷ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
